slides.headline: He led over 2,000 miners and laborers across a border - and got arrested for it. Twice.
On November 6, 1913, Mohandas Gandhi led roughly 2,221 Indian miners and laborers across the Natal-Transvaal border at Volksrust, South Africa.
slides.body: The non-violent march protested a discriminatory £3 tax on former indentured Indians and a law invalidating Hindu and Muslim marriages. Gandhi was arrested that day, released on bail, rejoined the march, and was arrested again.

slides.headline: The satyagraha campaign led directly to the Indian Relief Act of 1914, which scrapped the tax.
slides.body: It was one of the defining early demonstrations of organized, non-violent mass resistance - a method Gandhi would later bring home to India's own independence movement.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: A Viksit Bharat still draws on the idea that organized, disciplined resistance can change unjust laws without violence.
slides.body: The Volksrust march is a reminder that India's influence on global movements for justice predates its own independence by decades.
